pages.title: Welcome to Hebleo
pages.html:
Welcome to Hebleo, the smart way to learn Hebrew. This course is the result of a 10+ year long journey, combining many years of experience in:

Learning languages independently on a self-paced basis and seeing what works and what doesn’t first-hand,

Teaching Hebrew as a tutor and developing materials along the way, optimizing them with each new student with different approaches, and seeing what works well long-term

Getting an M.Sc. in Cognitive Science. It has helped me understand how to optimize learning in general and language learning in particular.

pages.title: Adam
pages.html:
This led to a case study I did with a student named Adam. He came to me with Zero Hebrew knowledge, but similar scientific background. After I explained the method to him, he became intrigued and we decided to test how long it would take him to get to a level where we would be able to generally hold Hebrew conversations together. For an English speaker learning Hebrew, this usually takes around 500 hours. For Adam, using the methodology that is at the core of Hebleo, it took around 70 hours. This means that his pace was over 7x higher than the norm.

Let’s briefly demonstrate some of the underlying concepts used in the course that improve your learning and memory. Understanding them can help you use them in your personal life as well!

pages.title: A quick memory experiment
pages.html:
Let’s try a quick experiment. I’m going to show you a number for ten seconds. Try to remember as much of it as you can without writing it down. When it disappears, type what you remember.

Ready? Press Play to begin.
pages.prompt: How much of the number can you remember? Enter whatever comes to mind, or select Show me how.

feedback.partial: That was a lot of digits to hold in mind! Let me show you a way to make sense of them.
feedback.exact: You remembered it. Now let me show you a way to organise the same information.

pages.title: Give the number meaning
pages.html: That was quite a lot of digits to remember! Most people can get up to half of it, and certainly wouldn’t remember it in 1 month. Now watch what happens when we think about the same number differently.

descriptions: The same digits, grouped into two sets of eight.
Slashes show the month, day and year within each group.
activity.after:
These dates use American month–day–year order: July 4, 1776, and September 11, 2001.

The first is the date of the American Declaration of Independence; the second is the date of the September 11 attacks. For most people, assuming these dates are familiar to you, not only would you easily remember them now, but would probably be able to recite them in order in a month.

We haven’t changed any of the digits though, so what changed?

What changed is our interpretation, or framing, of the information, which makes it easier to remember due to 3 concepts:

principles.title: Chunking:
principles.text: instead of trying to hold sixteen separate digits in mind, we can think of two meaningful units—the two dates. Each date still contains several digits, but we can treat it as one item.

principles.title: Logical constraints:
principles.text: a date has a structure, and that structure limits the possibilities. A month must be between 01 and 12, so 19 cannot be the month. A day cannot be 47. Knowing the format helps us rule out possibilities instead of treating every digit as completely open.

principles.title: Memory hooks:
principles.text: if you already know these events and their dates, the number connects to knowledge you already have. If the events are unfamiliar, this particular connection will be less useful to you, even though the grouping and date structure may still help.

pages.title: What made the difference?
pages.html:
While we’ll use all 3 principles to enhance our learning, right now I want to focus on the third one: connecting new information to established old information. You already have a great deal of knowledge to build on from your life experience. A useful connection gives the new information a place in that knowledge. At first we’ll connect brand new Hebrew concepts to things you’re already familiar with from English, and as we move forward we’ll connect new Hebrew concepts to older Hebrew concepts you’re already comfortable with.

All three principles will come back throughout the course. Let’s check what they mean in practice.
pages.prompt: Imagine you recognise the number as two dates, but neither event is familiar to you. What could still help you remember it?
options: Memorise the names of the three memory principles.
Use the two date groups and what you know about how dates work.
Attach an event name to each date, even if neither event means anything to you.

feedback: Knowing the names doesn’t help you recover these digits. Try using the grouping and date structure instead.
Yes. Two date groups give you larger units to work with, and the date format limits the possibilities. Those can still help even when the events are unfamiliar.
An unfamiliar event name adds something else to remember. A useful memory hook connects the new information to something you already know.

pages.title: Notice the difference (optional)
pages.html:
If you’d like to try the comparison, bring the number back to mind once more. Think of the two dates and enter what you remember, without looking back. You can also skip this step and continue to the next lesson.

If you try it, compare your attempts and notice whether grouping, the date format, or the familiar events helped. We’ll use the same ideas throughout the course, starting with familiar images that help us remember Hebrew letter shapes and sounds.
pages.prompt: With the two dates in mind, what can you now recall? Enter an attempt, select Show the comparison, or skip this step.

feedback.exact: That’s the original sequence. Notice which part of the connection helped you bring it back.
feedback.reverse: You recalled both dates, but swapped their order. The original starts with July 4, 1776, then September 11, 2001.
feedback.zeros: You recalled the dates. In the original display, months and days use two digits: 07/04 and 09/11. Those zeroes are part of the original sequence.
feedback.dayMonth: You used day–month–year. These are the same dates; the demonstration uses month–day–year, so its sequence begins 07/04/1776.
feedback.partial: Here’s the original number alongside your attempt. Compare the two date groups and notice which parts came back to you.
feedback.empty: Here are the two dates within the original number. Notice how the grouping, format and familiar events can help you make sense of it.

pages.title: Continue
pages.html: You’ve seen how grouping, logical constraints and familiar knowledge can make the same information easier to work with. Next, we’ll start with that third idea: using familiar concepts from English to help you learn your first four Hebrew letters. See you in the next lesson!

pages.title: Four shapes, four sounds
pages.html: Listen to each sound and look at its letter. The mountain-climber, nose, tripping and ladle pictures connect each printed shape to a familiar word that begins with its sound. You do not need to memorise the letter names yet.

items.text: מ represents /m/, the sound at the start of mountain. Its name is Mem.
נ represents /n/, the sound at the start of nose. Its name is Nun.
ת represents /t/, as at the start of tripping. Its name is Tav.
ל represents /l/, as at the start of ladle. Its name is Lamed.

pages.title: Try without the pictures
pages.html: Now try recognising a letter without its picture. If you need help, bring the familiar image back to mind.

feedback: מ represents /m/. The sound you heard was /n/.
Yes: נ represents /n/, as in nose.
ת represents /t/. The sound you heard was /n/.
ל represents /l/. The sound you heard was /n/.

pages.title: Make the shape yourself
pages.html:
Choose the matching printed letter on the Hebrew keyboard. You may use the on-screen keyboard.

Copying a visible shape helps you locate its key. In the next exercise, the shape will be hidden so that you can try to recall it.

activity.feedback: Correct: ל. Use the same printed form; handwriting is not required.

feedback: נ is /n/. Think of tripping for /t/.
מ is /m/. Think of tripping for /t/.
ל is /l/. Think of tripping for /t/.

pages.title: Match sounds and letters
pages.prompt: Match each sound to its printed letter.

activity.feedback: מ = /m/, נ = /n/, ת = /t/, ל = /l/. Replay a missed sound, then retry it without the mnemonic.

pages.title: Recall the printed letter
pages.prompt: Listen and type the printed letter.

activity.feedback: The matching letter is מ; its sound is /m/.

pages.title: Recall another letter
pages.prompt: Listen and type the printed letter.

activity.feedback: The matching letter is ל; its sound is /l/.

pages.title: Read aloud (optional)
pages.prompt: Read the sounds of these letters aloud: ל  מ  ת  נ.

activity.feedback: Reveal the four individual sound buttons and compare one at a time. This is self-check, not automatic pronunciation scoring.

pages.title: Continue
pages.html: You can now connect four printed letters to their sounds. Next, you will see how Hebrew arranges them and what happens to מ and נ at the end of a word.
